title: "Am I not your Lord?"
hook: the souls of Adam's children are asked, am I not your Lord, and say, yes (7:172)

segments.voice: Yesterday: arini, let me see You, and the mountain. Your line was the mountain could not bear it. A week ends today: no waste, a quiet du'a, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Musa on the mountain. Now a question older than all of them.
screen: `ARINI — THE MOUNTAIN COULD NOT BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: A song heard for the first time that seems already known. A street never walked before that somehow says, I know this. Persian poets had a name for an older version of that feeling: the day of Alast. They meant a moment before anyone was born, when every human soul heard a single question and gave a single answer. They took it from one verse in surah seven, and Alast is simply the first word of that question in Arabic.
screen: `A SONG YOU'VE ALWAYS KNOWN.` → `THE DAY OF ALAST.` → `ONE QUESTION, ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Verse one-seventy-two says your Lord brought out from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify about themselves. Then the question, in Pickthall's words: “Am I not your Lord? They said: Yea, verily. We testify.” In Arabic: alastu bi-rabbikum? Qalu bala. The verse gives the reason: so that no one can say on the Day of Resurrection, we didn't know about this. Scholars call this al-mithaq, the covenant, from a root meaning to bind firmly, like a rope tied tight; the word appears in the verses just before. What exactly happened? Muslim scholars read it two main ways. Some, citing a hadith in which Umar asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about this verse, take it as a real event: every soul drawn out and asked, before the world began. Others read it as a picture of human nature itself, the fitrah: every person made with knowledge of their Lord built in, the testimony written into who they are. Both readings agree on the most striking part. In this telling, faith isn't something foreign added later. It's remembering. Sufi poets took this up. Rumi wrote of the reed flute, cut from its reed bed, crying out to go home, and some readers hear in that the soul longing for the day it said yes. The Qur'an's own word for the answer is tiny: bala. Yes.
screen: `ALASTU BI-RABBIKUM?` · `QALU BALA — THEY SAID, YES.` · `AN EVENT, OR HUMAN NATURE?` · `FAITH AS REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `WE SAID YES.`

segments.voice: Imagine, just for a moment, that before your first breath you were asked a question and you answered; you don't have to decide what you believe about it, just sit inside the picture. Then, if it fits, let the word bala, yes, pass through your mind on one quiet out-breath, and if it doesn't, notice what in you wants to say yes to something larger.
Mithaq. The covenant: the firm pledge of 7:172, when the children of Adam were asked, am I not your Lord, and said, yes. Today's word.
Your line: we said yes. A familiar feeling can be a small remembering. Four hundred thirteen days now.

screen: `DAY 413 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CALL HIM BY HIS NAMES.`

howItsDone: Muslims teach 7:172 as the primordial covenant (al-mithaq) and link it to the fitrah, the natural disposition toward God; Sufi poets, especially in Persian, call it the day of Alast.

original.note: Arabic: a covenant, a firm pledge, from w-th-q, to bind firmly.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old story about souls.
what it means: the covenant of Alast: every person, in this telling, once said yes to their Lord, so faith is a remembering.
what a scholar hears: bala, not na'am, answers a negative question affirmatively; the hadith of Umar (Muwatta, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi) supports the literal reading, while others read 7:172 as fitrah.

chat.says: What's this 'day of Alast' the poets talk about?
options: From 7:172: Adam's children were asked, 'Am I not your Lord?' and said yes. Faith as remembering.
The day the Qur'an was first revealed, when the angel came and told the Prophet to read.
The last day of the world, when each soul is asked if it ever heard of God.
chat.meaning: Alastu bi-rabbikum? Qalu bala. Scholars read it as a real event or as human nature, the fitrah; both see faith as remembering.

mithaq.meaning: a covenant, a firm pledge; from a root meaning to bind

Alast.meaning: the first word of 'Am I not your Lord?'

bala.meaning: yes, answering a question asked in the negative

fitrah.meaning: human nature as created, knowing its Lord
